patient.chief_complaint: Neck drooping and head drop, mild dysphagia and dysphonia, with Parkinson-like features
patient.hpi:
A 73-year-old man presented to the neurology ward with a several-month history of progressive neck flexion weakness and an inability to hold his head upright. He described a gradual worsening of head drop over approximately 4 months such that he needed to manually support his chin when seated or walking. He also noted mild dysphagia for solids and a hoarse, quieter quality to his voice over the past 2 months. He denied ptosis, diplopia, limb weakness, or sensory symptoms. His family history was notable for Parkinson's disease in his father. He did not smoke or drink alcohol and was on no medications prior to admission.

His past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease (managed conservatively), and arterial hypertension, as well as mild cervical spondylosis identified on prior imaging. On neurological examination, he was alert with hypomimia, mild bilateral bradykinesia, and asymmetric limb rigidity. There was no ptosis or diplopia. Extraocular movements were full. Strength testing revealed profound 2/5 power in the neck extensor group bilaterally with preserved 5/5 strength in all four limbs, shoulder girdle, and hip girdle muscles. Cognition was intact (MMSE 28/30). Gait was slightly shuffling with mild festination.

Brain and cervical spine MRI studies showed no structural abnormalities — specifically no compressive pathology, no anterior spinal cord compression, and no signal change in the dorsal columns or anterior horn cells. The combination of isolated neck extensor weakness with preserved limb strength was felt to be highly atypical for Parkinson's disease, which prompted dedicated neuromuscular evaluation.
pmh: Mild cervical spondylosis on prior imaging

family_history: Father had Parkinson's disease; no family history of autoimmune or neuromuscular disease

social_history.note: Retired engineer; non-smoker; non-drinker; lives with wife; minimally active due to neck drop symptoms

physical_exam.general: Alert; hypomimia; head drop present — patient required chin support to maintain upright head posture
physical_exam.neurological: Alert; MMSE 28/30. No ptosis. No diplopia. Full extraocular movements. Hypomimia. Mild bilateral bradykinesia. Asymmetric rigidity (right > left). Neck extensors: 2/5 bilaterally (profound weakness — cannot maintain head against gravity). All other muscle groups: 5/5. No fasciculations. DTR 2+ symmetric. Sensation intact throughout. Slight festinating gait. MMSE intact.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.respiratory: Mild decreased breath sounds at right base

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: AChR antibody–positive generalized myasthenia gravis with isolated neck extensor predominance (head drop) (G70.01)

differential.key_features: PD antecollis is from increased axial tone (rigidity), not true muscular weakness; neck extensors 2/5 represents true weakness which is NOT a PD feature
differential.distinguishing_test: Bedside exam (2/5 neck extensors = true weakness); AChR antibody (positive)

differential.diagnosis: Inflammatory myopathy (IBM or isolated neck extensor myopathy)
differential.key_features: Normal CK (78 U/L); normal aldolase; no myopathic changes on needle EMG; RNS shows decremental pattern (NMJ, not myopathic)
differential.distinguishing_test: CK (normal), needle EMG (normal), RNS (NMJ decremental pattern)

differential.key_features: Mild spondylosis on MRI but no cord compression and no cord signal change; myelopathy would cause spastic weakness with hyperreflexia, not isolated neck drop
differential.distinguishing_test: MRI cervical spine (no myelopathy), normal reflexes

differential.diagnosis: ALS with early neck extensor involvement
differential.key_features: Normal needle EMG (no fasciculations or denervation); no tongue atrophy; no fasciculations; AChR positive

optimal_actions.action: Brain and cervical spine MRI to exclude structural cause (cervical myelopathy, brainstem lesion)
RNS of neck extensors and cranial muscles — most sensitive for neck extensor MG
AChR antibody panel — including binding, blocking, modulating
Initiate pyridostigmine; add prednisone with PPI and diabetes glucose monitoring intensification

critical_actions: Recognize that 2/5 neck extensor weakness is true muscular weakness — not Parkinson's antecollis (which is axial rigidity, not weakness)
RNS of neck extensor muscles is the most sensitive electrophysiological test for this presentation
AChR antibody 8.0 nmol/L is markedly elevated and diagnostic
Normal MRI cervical spine excludes cervical myelopathy as cause of neck drop
Prednisone will worsen T2DM — intensify glucose monitoring
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute neck drop to cervical spondylosis without confirming cord compression on MRI
Do not attribute neck drop to Parkinson's disease without demonstrating increased axial tone (not weakness)
Do not prescribe fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides
Do not routinely perform thymectomy in patients >65 without thymoma without multidisciplinary discussion
key_reasoning_points: The pivotal distinction: Parkinson's antecollis = increased anterior cervical TONE (rigidity); MG neck drop = isolated neck extensor WEAKNESS (2/5) — these are fundamentally different mechanisms
Isolated neck extensor weakness in an elderly man with Parkinson-like features should prompt NMJ evaluation
Normal needle EMG (no fasciculations) excludes ALS; normal CK excludes inflammatory myopathy
RNS of neck extensors showing 19% decrement is the key electrophysiological finding
AChR antibody 8.0 nmol/L with anti-titin positive in a 73-year-old fits late-onset MG without thymoma

red_herrings.finding: Parkinson-like features (hypomimia, bradykinesia, rigidity) suggesting antecollis from Parkinson's disease
red_herrings.why_misleading: Parkinson's antecollis (dropped head from forward flexion) is a known PD complication; combined with family history, PD antecollis is strongly suggested
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: PD antecollis is from axial rigidity of anterior neck, not true extensor weakness; 2/5 neck extensors is MG weakness — not PD

red_herrings.why_misleading: Cervical spondylosis with neck problems could explain head drop from myelopathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: No cord compression, no signal change on MRI; myelopathy excluded; spondylosis is an incidental finding

red_herrings.finding: Atorvastatin as potential cause of myopathy
red_herrings.why_misleading: Statin myopathy can cause neck weakness; patient is on atorvastatin
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal CK (78 U/L); statin myopathy causes myopathic EMG pattern and elevated CK; RNS shows NMJ pattern not myopathic pattern; AChR antibody is diagnostic

metadata.condition_name: Late-onset AChR+ MG presenting as isolated head drop with Parkinson-like comorbidity
metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward: isolated 2/5 neck extensor weakness with disproportionality to PD features; RNS decrement + AChR antibody 8.0 nmol/L are diagnostic; distinguishing MG weakness from PD antecollis rigidity is the key clinical step

mri.impression: No cervical myelopathy; mild nigral changes (parkinsonism); no structural cause for neck extensor weakness. Clinical correlation recommended.

additional_observations:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: Newly suspected MG — thymoma screen

FINDINGS: No anterior mediastinal mass. Thymic involution appropriate for age. No lung mass. No mediastinal adenopathy.

IMPRESSION: Normal chest CT. No thymoma.

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION — NECK EXTENSOR AND CRANIAL NERVE INNERVATED MUSCLES

Indication: Isolated neck extensor weakness; exclude NMJ disorder

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS at the neck extensor muscle (C2-C4 accessory-cervical innervation), trapezius, and nasalis

RESULTS:
  Neck extensor: Reduction in compound muscle action potential amplitude and area between 1st and 4th stimuli: 19% decrement ABNORMAL
  Trapezius: Decrement 16% ABNORMAL
  Nasalis: Decrement 12% ABNORMAL
  Abductor digiti minimi (ulnar): Decrement 5% NORMAL

NEEDLE EMG: No fibrillations, no fasciculations, no myopathic changes in neck extensors or limb muscles.

CONCLUSION: Abnormal decremental response in neck extensor and proximal cranial muscles with normal distal limb muscles. Pattern consistent with generalized MG with preferential neck extensor involvement. No myopathic features on needle EMG.

specialized_test.impression: RNS: 19% decrement neck extensors, 16% trapezius, 12% nasalis; normal needle EMG — MG pattern with neck predominance confirmed

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — EXTENSOR DIGITORUM COMMUNIS

MCD: 72 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
Blocking: 26% of potential pairs

CONCLUSION: SFEMG confirms NMJ dysfunction. Consistent with generalized MG.

output.impression: SFEMG: MCD 72 µs with 26% blocking — markedly abnormal; confirms NMJ dysfunction

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Isolated Neck Extensor Weakness (Head Drop) as MG Presentation

KEY FINDINGS:
1. DROPPED HEAD SYNDROME: Causes include ALS (bulbar onset), myopathy (isolated neck extensor myopathy, IBM, mitochondrial), Parkinson's disease antecollis, and MG
2. PARKINSON'S ANTECOLLIS vs MG NECK DROP: PD antecollis is from increased axial tone (rigidity) of anterior cervical muscles, not weakness; true weakness (2/5 neck extensors) is NOT a feature of PD
3. MG NECK EXTENSOR PREDOMINANCE: Late-onset MG (>60) with anti-AChR or anti-MuSK can preferentially affect neck extensors; head drop is the first presentation in ~2-3% of MG cases
4. DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: RNS of neck extensors is more sensitive than limb RNS; AChR antibody is key; response to pyridostigmine is typically positive
5. CERVICAL MYELOPATHY vs MG NECK DROP: Myelopathy causes cord compression — excluded by normal MRI; MG causes pure muscular weakness without cord pathology

CONCLUSION: MG neck drop is confirmed by RNS, AChR antibody, and absence of myelopathy. Pyridostigmine initiation typically results in significant improvement within days.
output.summary: MG neck drop is a recognized but rare presentation; PD antecollis from rigidity not weakness; RNS neck extensors and AChR antibody are key

output.report:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — ATORVASTATIN AND MG

Query: Statin myopathy vs MG; interaction of atorvastatin with pyridostigmine

FINDINGS:
  ATORVASTATIN + MG:
  - Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) can cause myopathy and rhabdomyolysis
  - CK was normal in this patient (78 U/L) — statin myopathy unlikely
  - However, statins have also been reported to unmask or exacerbate MG in case reports
  - Clinical decision: Continue atorvastatin given established CAD benefit; monitor CK

  ATORVASTATIN + PYRIDOSTIGMINE:
  - No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction
  - Both are safe to co-administer

  ATORVASTATIN + AZATHIOPRINE:
  - No significant interaction; monitor LFTs when azathioprine is added

CONCLUSION: Continue atorvastatin (CAD indication outweighs theoretical MG risk given normal CK). Monitor CK during initial MG treatment period.
output.summary: Atorvastatin safe to continue (normal CK, CAD indication); no interaction with pyridostigmine; monitor CK

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: MGTX Trial and Thymectomy in Late-Onset MG

MGTX TRIAL (Wolfe GI et al., NEJM 2016):
  - Enrolled: AChR+ generalized MG patients 18-65 years
  - Results: Thymectomy + prednisone significantly better than prednisone alone (lower QMG score, lower prednisone dose, fewer treatment failures)
  - This patient: Age 73 — exceeds MGTX trial age range of 65
  - No thymoma: CT chest normal
  - Expert consensus: Benefit of thymectomy in patients >65 without thymoma is less well established; guidelines recommend case-by-case multidisciplinary decision

CURRENT RECOMMENDATION:
  - Age 73: MGTX trial evidence is extrapolated — benefit less certain than in <65
  - Surgical risk in elderly: higher perioperative risk with coronary artery disease
  - Recommendation: Discuss with thoracic surgery; weigh risk of surgery against expected immunosuppression benefit; initiate pyridostigmine + prednisone first and reassess

CONCLUSION: Thymectomy is not routinely recommended at age 73 without thymoma; initiate medical MG management first.
output.summary: MGTX trial age limit 65; thymectomy less established for age 73 without thymoma; medical management first; multidisciplinary discussion
